title: Head‑to‑head Evaluation of Translation‑First vs Agentic Generate→Validate→Repair Pipelines for Intent‑Driven NetOps Changes — Validator‑Acceptance Parity under Shared‑Candidate Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) comparing two operational architectures for intent→configuration NetOps changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and Mininet‑derived topologies: (A) translation‑first (constrained vendor DSL → formal verifier → solver) and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair (hosted LLM + deterministic validators). The run used gpt‑5‑mini for generation and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for deterministic end‑to‑end correctness checks; preregistration used shared_initial_candidate semantics so each task pair received a single LLM candidate shared between arms. Execution completed 240 episodes (120 paired tasks) with one shared generation per pair (model_calls_used = 120). Deterministic scoring produced contingency counts n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (baseline = 120/120; guarded = 120/120). Paired difference (A − B) = 0.00; paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Because generation was intentionally shared, these outcomes measure validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates rather than independent generator or repair robustness. We add an explicit provider‑call contamination audit: representative provider_call artifacts are archived (execution/provider_calls/task-000001-shared-initial.json, task-000002-shared-initial.json, task-000003-shared-initial.json) and preregistered automated contamination checks (analysis/contamination_summary.csv) produced no flags. We include a compact artifact‑grounded example (provider_call path → shared candidate → scoring JSON fields) and explain how the audit ruled out prompt leakage of canonical references. The archived bundle contains full per‑task prompts, responses, validator traces, and analysis artifacts supporting every numeric claim.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation and safe sequencing of multi‑vendor NetOps changes is operationally critical: production networks require both deterministic correctness guarantees (reachability, isolation, absence of transient safety violations) and flexibility to express diverse intents across vendor CLIs. Two architectural approaches are common: (A) translation‑first pipelines that restrict generation to a vendor DSL and apply formal verification/solvers, and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair pipelines that centralize generation in an LLM and rely on deterministic validators plus bounded repair. Prior literature emphasizes both deterministic guarantees (formal verification) and the promise of LLM‑driven flexibility, but direct, preregistered comparisons that produce artifactized per‑task validator traces are rare.

This study asked a preregistered head‑to‑head question: for intent‑driven network changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and realistic emulator topologies, which architecture yields higher end‑to‑end operational correctness (measured by deterministic validation of reachability/isolation) — (A) translation‑first or (B) agentic generate→validate→repair? The preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) fixed a paired design (N = 120 paired tasks), the primary estimand (paired difference A − B), the generator (gpt‑5‑mini), the deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and the analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1). A decisive design choice was shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each pair the system generated a single LLM candidate and supplied that identical candidate to both architectures. This choice intentionally isolates downstream acceptance behavior (validator/orchestrator parity) and eliminates generator variance from the confirmatory estimand. The remainder of the paper explicitly maps preregistered hypotheses to this restricted estimand and reports artifact‑grounded evidence.
sections.related_work: Two research traditions frame our contribution: (1) formal translation and verification systems that prioritize deterministic guarantees, and (2) LLM‑driven agentic NetOps work that emphasizes flexible generation and iterative repair. Formal translation→verification systems (e.g., SymNet and subsequent verification frameworks) impose a constrained DSL and apply symbolic/solver checks to obtain binary acceptance and counterexamples [10,11]. LLM‑driven NetOps research instruments generate→validate→repair loops, records repair traces, and measures repair coverage and transient unsafe proposals [3,4]. These literatures differ along four experimental axes used throughout this paper: independent generation sampling, repair‑loop instrumentation, validator‑acceptance focus, and emulator/hardware realism. Our preregistered shared_candidate design places this run squarely on the validator‑acceptance axis: it asks whether downstream orchestration and verification produce different deterministic verdicts for identical LLM candidates. Nearest works that perform independent sampling or instrument repair loops are complementary; to test those hypotheses one must change generation semantics and resource budgets (see Methods and Discussion).
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and core contract. The preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) froze the primary estimand (paired binary difference A − B), N_confirmatory = 120 paired tasks, generator = gpt‑5‑mini, validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0), adapter_family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1, maximum_model_calls = 240, and shared_initial_candidate semantics. Analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1 (bootstrap percentile CIs, exact McNemar test). The preregistration artifact is archived and its checksum is recorded in the execution manifest.

Task corpus and canonical references. Confirmatory tasks (120 pairs) were generated deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Each manifest entry archives intent text, a canonical reference answer (normalized configuration), initial and expected final states, required safe sequences, and difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, level). Representative manifest entries and canonical references are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and per‑task manifest entries (e.g., pair‑000001) are available in the artifact bundle.

Shared_initial_candidate generation semantics. The orchestration implemented a single LLM generation per pair that was supplied identically to both downstream arms (translation‑first and agentic). Execution accounting records planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, and model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair) in execution/execution_manifest.json. Provider audit (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) reports hosted_model_call_event_count = 120 and cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false, consistent with execution isolation.

Deterministic validator and scoring. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applies full_intent_constraint_validation: syntactic normalization, required command inclusion, ordering/dependency checks (make‑before‑break, shutdown→modify→restore), final state consistency, and a boolean validation_after.valid flag. A configuration is scored success (1) only when validation_after.valid == true. Per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task‑000XXX‑*.json) record normalized_response, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, validation_before/after snapshots, repair_applied flags and the scorer id/version; these files are the canonical evidence for per‑task decisions and are archived.

Provider‑call contamination audit (added per peer review). Preregistered contamination checks were executed against provider_call artifacts; representative provider_call files for this paper are archived at execution/provider_calls/task-000001-shared-initial.json, execution/provider_calls/task-000002-shared-initial.json, and execution/provider_calls/task-000003-shared-initial.json. The automated contamination detector (preregistered in the contamination_plan) searches provider_call payloads for any occurrence of the canonical reference_answer string and for unexpected inclusion of reference fields in model prompt bodies. The contamination report (analysis/contamination_summary.csv) contains zero flags (empty), indicating no detected prompt contamination for the confirmatory set. To make the linkage concrete we present a compact, artifact‑grounded example below (Representative example). The full provider_call artifacts and the contamination_check code and outputs are archived in the execution bundle referenced by the execution manifest; these archives contain the exact prompt payloads used for generation for independent verification.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary numeric outcomes. The execution manifest records planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 120 (one shared LLM call per paired task), and maximum_model_calls = 240. Deterministic reconciliation (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) confirms complete_pair_count = 120 and provider audit counts consistent with one generation per pair.

Primary contingency and inference. The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Marginal success rates are baseline = 120/120 = 1.0 and guarded = 120/120 = 1.0; the observed paired difference A − B = 0.00. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI was computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) and returned [0.00, 0.00]. The exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.0. These statistics follow directly from the degenerate contingency and are archived (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv).

Repair and secondary outcomes. Across all 240 episodes per‑task scoring traces record repair_applied = false (execution/scoring/*.json). Consequently preregistered secondary estimands that quantify repair coverage and mean repair iterations are unobserved in this execution; the absence of repairs is itself an archived experimental result (analysis/condition_summary.csv and per‑task scoring JSONs).

Representative example (artifact‑grounded). To illustrate the provider_call → shared candidate → validator chain with explicit artifact references, consider pair‑000001: the model response archive (execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt) contains the shared candidate text:

interface edge1 admin down
interface edge1 vlan 30
interface edge1 mtu 1600
interface edge1 admin up

The corresponding scoring artifact (execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json and execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json) records parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, validation_after.valid = true, and repair_applied = false. The provider_call artifact that contains the exact generation payload is archived at execution/provider_calls/task-000001-shared-initial.json; the preregistered contamination detector scanned those provider_call payloads for any literal inclusion of the canonical reference_answer and produced no flags (analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty). Similar provider_call → response → scoring chains are archived for task‑000002 and task‑000003 (execution/provider_calls/task-000002-shared-initial.json, execution/responses/task-000002-shared-initial.txt, execution/scoring/task-000002-*.json; and the analogous set for task‑000003). These artifacts together demonstrate that the shared candidate was the model output actually validated and that the validator decisions are recorded in the scoring JSONs.

Contamination and missingness diagnostics. The preregistered contamination checks produced no flags (analysis/contamination_summary.csv empty). Missingness diagnostics report complete_pairs = 120 and zero failed episodes (analysis/missingness_summary.csv). Provider audit and execution logs show no retries or infrastructure failures beyond the planned single generation per pair.

Statistical note. The degenerate contingency (perfect concordance) produces a point mass CI and p = 1.0; this is a correct reflection of the observed data under the preregistered estimand. Because the design fixed shared candidates the result measures validator‑acceptance parity rather than generator or repair performance.
sections.discussion:
Measured estimand and bounds on inference. The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics intentionally remove generator variance; accordingly this run answers the narrower question: when supplied identical LLM candidates, do downstream translation‑first and agentic orchestration/verification paths produce different deterministic validator outcomes? The observed complete concordance (n11 = 120) answers this restricted question in the negative for the chosen model, validator, and task corpus: both arms accepted the identical candidates in every paired task.

Why concordance occurred. Artifact traces show that many shared candidates matched canonical reference answers after normalization (see representative example). The task generator encodes required_sequence and canonical references; the validator enforces required_command_count and ordering constraints. In this execution the normalized shared candidates satisfied those constraints, yielding validation_after.valid = true and no repair invocation. The per‑task scoring JSONs are the mechanistic link between generation and acceptance and are archived for audit.

How to obtain a discriminating comparison (preregistered recommendations). To test the original broader hypotheses about generator robustness and repair efficacy the preregistration must be changed to exercise generator variance and repair loops: (i) remove shared_initial_candidate so each arm receives independent LLM generations (model_calls_used increases to 240 for initial candidates); (ii) enable independent sampling or multiple initial draws per arm; (iii) enable and instrument repair iterations so repair_applied can be nonzero and secondary estimands observed; (iv) optionally increase emulator fidelity or include hardware runs to reduce simulator/hardware divergence risk. Each modification produces distinct archived signatures: higher hosted_model_call_event_count, nonzero repair_applied counts in execution/scoring/*.json, and a nondegenerate paired contingency.

Threats to validity and construct nuances. Internal validity: the shared_candidate design reduces variance by construction and therefore increases internal consistency for the validator‑parity estimand. Construct validity: the binary deterministic acceptance metric is a conservative operational gate, but per‑task parsed counts, violation codes, and validation_before/after snapshots archived in execution/scoring/*.json enable richer graded analyses while preserving a deployment gate. External validity: the synthetic Mininet‑derived corpus, single model (gpt‑5‑mini), and single deterministic validator limit generality; these constraints are explicit in the preregistration and in the Limitations section. Conclusion validity: with a degenerate contingency the exact tests and bootstrap CI reflect the point mass; that outcome is reproducibly recorded in the archived analysis artifacts.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, artifactized paired experiment comparing translation‑first and agentic generate→validate→repair NetOps pipelines under shared_initial_candidate semantics. For 120 paired tasks deterministic validators accepted identical LLM candidates in both arms for every pair (n11 = 120), yielding paired difference 0.00 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.00], McNemar p = 1.0). No repairs were applied (repair_applied = false throughout); preregistered hypotheses about repair coverage are therefore unobserved. The run precisely measures validator‑acceptance parity under controlled shared candidates, archives per‑task provider_call, response, and scoring artifacts (representative paths: execution/provider_calls/task-000001-shared-initial.json, execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt, execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json), documents that automated contamination checks produced no flags (analysis/contamination_summary.csv), and describes concrete protocol changes to enable discriminating follow‑ups that exercise independent generation and repair coverage.

limitations: Preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics were used; this intentionally removes generator variance and prevents this run from assessing independent generation robustness differences between architectures.

The task corpus was synthetic and executed in an emulator (Mininet‑derived topologies and public vendor example grammars); emulator‑to‑hardware divergence limits external validity to production devices.
A single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) were used; results do not imply multi‑model or multi‑validator generality.
No repairs were applied in this run (repair_applied = false in per‑task traces); preregistered secondary estimands about repair coverage remain unobserved for this execution.

The binary deterministic validator acceptance metric does not capture operator‑facing properties such as explanation quality, maintainability, or human trust, which matter in production but were outside the metric used here.
